questions.subject: Commerce
questions.prompt: A student is drafting a business plan and wants to add a SWOT analysis. Which section of the plan is the correct home for it?
options: A standalone section analysing internal Strengths/Weaknesses and external Opportunities/Threats
The executive summary, replacing the one-page overview
The financial plan, replacing cash flow forecasts
The market analysis, replacing customer and competitor research
questions.answer: A standalone section analysing internal Strengths/Weaknesses and external Opportunities/Threats
questions.why: SWOT is its own tool for weighing internal factors (strengths/weaknesses) against external ones (opportunities/threats) — it doesn't replace the market analysis, executive summary, or financials, which each have their own specific job.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: The Weimar Republic refers to which period of German history?
options: Germany's democratic government from 1919 to 1933
The Kaiser's empire before WWI
Nazi Germany from 1933 to 1945
Germany after WWII split into East and West
questions.why: The Weimar Republic was the name for Germany's first democracy, set up after WWI in 1919 and ending when Hitler took power in 1933.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: Why did the Great Depression make ordinary Germans more willing to vote for the Nazi Party?
options: Mass unemployment and poverty made extreme promises of recovery and strong leadership appealing
Germans had always supported Hitler and the Depression changed nothing
The Depression only affected other countries, not Germany
The Nazis caused the Depression, so people voted for them out of guilt
questions.answer: Mass unemployment and poverty made extreme promises of recovery and strong leadership appealing
questions.why: Economic desperation made the Weimar government look weak and made Hitler's promises of jobs, order, and strong leadership far more attractive to struggling voters.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.prompt: A wave of skilled workers moves from the UK to Australia after WWII, drawn by government-assisted passage schemes. Which factor is this an example of?
options: A pull factor, because opportunity in the destination drew them
A push factor, because conditions at home forced them out
Urbanisation, because it describes city growth
A push factor, because Australia had no role in it
questions.answer: A pull factor, because opportunity in the destination drew them
questions.why: Pull factors are things that attract migrants to a new place, like assisted passage and job opportunities — the scheme actively drew people to Australia rather than driving them from the UK.

questions.subject: Commerce
questions.prompt: A café redesigns its logo to use earthy green tones and a hand-drawn leaf icon. What is this logo mainly doing?
options: Building brand identity by visually communicating the business's values
Legally protecting the business from competitors
Replacing the need for a market analysis
Setting the price of the café's products
questions.answer: Building brand identity by visually communicating the business's values
questions.why: A logo is a branding tool — its colours and imagery are chosen to communicate what the business stands for (like being natural or eco-friendly) and to make it recognisable to customers.

questions.subject: Commerce
questions.prompt: A hairdresser gives a customer a haircut. Which best describes what's being sold?
options: A service, because it's an intangible action performed for the customer
A product, because it's a physical item the customer keeps
Both a product and a service equally, with no meaningful difference
Neither, because no exchange of money occurs
questions.answer: A service, because it's an intangible action performed for the customer
questions.why: Services are intangible actions or skills performed for a customer, while products are tangible items you can hold — a haircut is an action, not a physical good, so it's a service.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: How did the Treaty of Versailles act as a causal lever leading toward Hitler's rise?
options: Its harsh terms created resentment and economic hardship that Hitler exploited for support
It gave Germany extra territory, making people support the government
It had no real effect on Germany's economy or politics
It directly installed Hitler as Chancellor in 1919
questions.answer: Its harsh terms created resentment and economic hardship that Hitler exploited for support
questions.why: The Treaty's reparations, war guilt clause, and territorial losses crushed Germany's economy and pride, creating the resentment that Hitler later used to rally support and blame the Weimar government.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.prompt: A triangle has base 14 cm and height 6 cm. What is its area? Take your time — work through ½ × base × height calmly.
options: 42 cm²
84 cm²
40 cm²
20 cm²
questions.why: Area of a triangle is ½ × base × height = ½ × 14 × 6 = 42 cm². Rushing often causes skipping the ½, or misreading which numbers are the base and height — go step by step.

questions.subject: Commerce
questions.prompt: Which of the following would correctly belong INSIDE a SWOT analysis for a new bakery, rather than in the market analysis section?
options: A threat: a large supermarket chain opening nearby with cheaper bread
A description of the target customers' age and income
A survey of how many competing bakeries exist in the suburb
An estimate of total local demand for baked goods
questions.answer: A threat: a large supermarket chain opening nearby with cheaper bread
questions.why: SWOT captures strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats — a competitor threat fits SWOT, whereas customer profiles, competitor counts, and demand estimates belong in the market analysis.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: Which statement best captures why the Weimar Republic struggled to gain public trust from its very beginning?
options: It was blamed for accepting the humiliating Treaty of Versailles, seen by many as a betrayal
It was extremely popular and faced no serious opposition
It abolished elections almost immediately
It was set up by the Kaiser to strengthen his own power
questions.answer: It was blamed for accepting the humiliating Treaty of Versailles, seen by many as a betrayal
questions.why: The Weimar government signed the Treaty of Versailles, and many Germans saw this as a 'stab in the back', undermining trust in the new democracy from the start.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: Rank how confidently you'd explain this: rising unemployment during the Great Depression is best linked to Hitler's growing support because it…
options: Made desperate voters turn to extreme parties promising quick solutions
Made the Nazi Party promise to keep the Weimar government exactly as it was
Had no link — Hitler's support grew for unrelated reasons
Convinced voters that Weimar democracy was working well
questions.answer: Made desperate voters turn to extreme parties promising quick solutions
questions.why: Mass unemployment discredited the Weimar government's ability to cope, pushing many voters towards the Nazis, who promised jobs, national pride, and decisive action.
